questions: Did the facial weakness begin suddenly, reaching its worst within minutes?
Do you have weakness or numbness in an arm or leg?
Do you have difficulty speaking or understanding speech?
Do you have difficulty swallowing?
Do you have trouble walking, coordinating your movements, or maintaining your balance?
Do you have new double vision or loss of vision?
Do you have a sudden, severe headache?
Has the facial weakness continued to worsen since it began?
Did the weakness involve your forehead and difficulty closing your eye from the beginning?
Do you have severe pain in or behind the affected ear?
Do you have blisters or a rash in or around the affected ear or on that side of your face?
Have you noticed reduced hearing, ringing in the ear, or spinning dizziness?
Have you noticed a reduced sense of taste?
Have ordinary sounds seemed unusually loud in the affected ear?
Have you recently had a cold, flu-like illness, or COVID-19?
Have you recently had a tick bite or spent time in an area where Lyme disease is common?
Have you had an injury, surgery, or injection near the ear, face, or neck recently?
Have you had a similar episode of facial weakness before?
Do you have severe eye pain, marked light sensitivity, or blurred vision in the affected eye?
Do you have a mass or swelling near the ear, jaw, or side of the face?

results: 1. Complete neurological examination, including detailed cranial-nerve examination
cranial nerve examination: failure to adduct the right eye
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
visual acuity and colour vision: normal
ocular motility examination: failure to adduct the right eye
pupil examination (size, light reaction): equal and reactive
4. Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining of the left cornea
5. Assessment of left corneal sensation and Bell’s phenomenon
7. MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals with and without gadolinium contrast
MRI brain with contrast: no lesion, no cranial nerve enhancement
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Post-viral idiopathic left peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell palsy)

Alternative 1: Multiple sclerosis with a left facial palsy and right internuclear ophthalmoplegia

Alternative 2: Neuroborreliosis (Lyme disease) causing multiple cranial neuropathies

Alternative 3: Neurosarcoidosis causing multiple cranial neuropathies
order_raw:
1. Complete neurological examination, including detailed cranial-nerve examination
2. Visual-acuity testing in each eye
3. Pupillary examination and ocular-motility testing
4. Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining of the left cornea
5. Assessment of left corneal sensation and Bell’s phenomenon
6. Dilated fundus examination
7. MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals with and without gadolinium contrast
8. Nerve-conduction studies and facial-nerve electromyography
dx: Post-viral idiopathic left peripheral facial nerve palsy (Bell palsy)
